A life net was formerly used by firefighters to allow people on upper floors of a burning building to jump to safety. Its practical height limit was about six storeys, although some people survived jumps from an eight-storey building with varying injuries. When a person hits the net, it deforms and brings the person to rest over a longer time than a solid ground would.

(a) A person falls from 12 m above a life net with negligible initial speed. Neglect air resistance and the person’s size. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)

(i) Estimate (1) the vertical speed v and (2) the time of fall t just before the person reaches the net. (4 marks)

(ii) If the 70 kg person is stopped in 0.3 s, estimate the average force exerted on the person by the net. (3 marks)

(iii) What form of energy is stored by the life net while the falling person is being decelerated? (1 mark)

(b) (i) Give a reason why there is a height limit for using life nets. (1 mark)

(ii) A falling person might hit the rim, injuring the person or the firefighters. Explain why it is not easy for a person jumping from a height to reach the central part of the net. (2 marks)
2019|paper-1b|3.official:
(a)(i)(1) ½mv2 = mgh. [1M] v2 = 2(9.81)(12); v = 15.344054 m s−1 ≈ 15.3 m s−1. [1A] For g = 10 m s−2, v = 15.491933 ≈ 15.5 m s−1. Accept 15–15.5 m s−1.

(a)(i)(2) s = ½gt2. [1M] 12 = ½(9.81)t2; t = 1.564124 s ≈ 1.56 s. [1A] For g = 10 m s−2, t = 1.5491933 s ≈ 1.55 s. Accept 1.5–1.6 s.

(a)(ii) F − mg = ma. F = 70(15.3 − 0)/0.3 + 70 × 9.81. [1M+1M] F = 4266.9793 N ≈ 4270 N. [1A] For g = 10 m s−2, F = 4314.7845 N ≈ 4310 N. Accept 4180–4320 N. F = ma: 1M; F = ma + mg: 2M.

(a)(iii) Elastic potential energy. [1A] MUST include “elastic”; accept elastic energy.

(b)(i) Velocity is too high, hence force for deceleration is too large. Any ONE [1A]: the life net may be torn; the falling person may be injured; the firemen may not be able to hold the life net tight. Answer must give a consequence due to limitations of the net, person or firemen. Do not accept merely: force exceeds net’s limit; net is not strong enough to withstand force; force too large for the man to withstand.

(b)(ii) There exists a horizontal velocity when a person jumps [1A] and horizontal displacement is difficult to estimate as it depends on the time of fall, which is usually long. [1A] First mark: horizontal velocity/projectile motion; second: difficulty estimating horizontal displacement/direction.
2019|paper-1b|3.reasoning:
(a)(i) v = √(2gh) = 15.3 m s-1 and t = √(2h/g) = 1.56 s.
(ii) Upward net force gives F − mg = mΔv/Δt, so F = 70(15.3/0.3) + 70g ≈ 4.27 kN.
(iii) The net stores elastic potential energy.
(b)(i) From excessive height, impact speed and stopping force may injure the person/firefighters or tear the net.
(ii) A jumper has uncertain horizontal velocity; with a long fall time, the resulting horizontal displacement is difficult to predict.

Space station S is in a circular orbit 400 km above Earth. A spacecraft is launched from A at Earth’s surface at 8.02 km s⁻¹ and coasts with its engine off along elliptical orbit AB, whose major axis is AB, to meet S at B. The two orbits lie in the same plane.

Given: GM = 4 × 10⁵ km³ s⁻²; radius of Earth = 6400 km.

(a) (i) Using conservation of total mechanical energy, or otherwise, find the spacecraft speed vB at B. (2 marks)

(ii) Show that the spacecraft takes about 2663 s to travel from A to B. (2 marks)

(iii) Explain why an astronaut in the orbiting spacecraft experiences weightlessness. (1 mark)

(b) Station S travels at 7.67 km s⁻¹ with period 5570 s.

(i) If the spacecraft meets S exactly at B, use (a)(ii) to show that their initial angular separation θ is slightly less than 8°. (2 marks)

(ii) A student suggests slightly adjusting the launch speed at A so that vB exactly equals the station speed at B. Comment on feasibility. (2 marks)

(iii) Suggest one simple way for the spacecraft at B to attain the station’s speed. (1 mark)
2019|paper-2|1.S.official:
(a)(i) ½m(vB2 − vA2) = GMm(1/rB − 1/rA). vB2 − 8.022 = 2(4 × 105)[1/(6400 + 400) − 1/6400]. [1M, correct substitution for vA, rA, rB] vB = 7.547679036 km s−1 ≈ 7.55 km s−1. [1A]

(a)(ii) T = 2πa/v and GMm/a2 = mv2/a. ∴ T2 = 4π2a3/(GM). [1M, correct expression/derivation for Kepler’s third law] T = 2π√[a3/(GM)], where a = (rA + rB)/2 for elliptical orbit. a = [6400 + (400 + 6400)]/2 = 6600 km. [1M, correct semi-major axis] TAB = T/2 = ½{2π√[66003/(4 × 105)]} = 2663.3962 s ≈ 2663 s.

(a)(iii) Any ONE [1A]: gravitational force on astronaut is all used for accelerating astronaut; astronaut and spacecraft are under same acceleration due to gravity, i.e. free falling; gravitational force/weight on astronaut is all used for centripetal force. Do not accept merely same acceleration, acceleration of gravity used for centripetal force, or no normal reaction on astronaut.

(b)(i) θ = [(5570/2 − 2663)/5570] × 360°. [1M] = 7.8850987° ≈ 7.89°. [1A] Accept 7.8–7.9°. Alternatives: 2663/5570 = (180° − θ)/360°; [2π(6800)/7.67] × (180° − θ)/360° = 2663; θ = ωΔt = (2π/5570)(5570/2 − 2663) = (1.128 × 10−3 rad s−1)(122 s).

(b)(ii) If launching speed at A is slightly higher/lower, elliptical orbit’s major axis is longer/shorter, i.e. orbit changes. [1A] Thus two orbits no longer touch at B. [1A] Accept: shape of spacecraft orbit changes so two orbits cannot meet at B.

(b)(iii) Fire rocket briefly at B to boost speed from 7.55 km s−1 to required 7.67 km s−1. [1A] Error carried forward from (a)(i): if speed greater than 7.67 km s−1, slow spacecraft by reverse firing.
2019|paper-2|1.S.reasoning:
(a)(i) Conserving mechanical energy between rA = 6400 km and rB = 6800 km gives vB2 − 8.022 = 2GM(1/rB − 1/rA), so vB = 7.55 km s-1.
(ii) The ellipse has a = (6400+6800)/2 = 6600 km; T = 2π√(a3/GM) = 5326 s, so A→B takes T/2 = 2663 s.
(iii) Astronaut and spacecraft are in the same free fall, so no support force is felt.
(b)(i) The station turns (2663/5570)360° = 172.1°, leaving θ = 180°−172.1° = 7.9°.
(ii) Changing launch speed changes the ellipse and its meeting point, so it cannot simply match the speed at B.
